cosy-lesson.title: Why Are We Obsessed with Celebrity Memorial Photos on Social Media?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Parasocial grief ≠ Private mourning – emotional sorrow felt for a public figure one never personally knew ≠ intimate grieving for a personal relation.

p.em: Example: Social media amplifies parasocial grief across global online communities, unlike private mourning shared only among close relatives.

cosy-blockquote.p: Performative tribute ≠ Sincere homage – a public display of respect intended primarily to gain online attention ≠ a genuine expression of admiration.

p.em: Example: Posting a stylized tribute photo often feels like a performative tribute rather than a sincere homage to the artist's work.

cosy-blockquote.p: Digital nostalgia ≠ Historical memory – sentimental longing for past pop culture eras created through online media feeds ≠ accurate recollection of past events.

p.em: Example: Short video edits generate a wave of digital nostalgia that often romanticizes complex historical eras.

cosy-blockquote.p: Posthumous reverence ≠ Lifetime appreciation – deep respect awarded to an artist only after their death ≠ recognizing and honoring talent while the person is alive.

p.em: Example: Many musicians suffer from neglect during their careers only to receive posthumous reverence decades later.

cosy-blockquote.p: Aestheticization ≠ Authentic portrayal – transforming real events or people into stylized visual objects ≠ depicting reality without superficial filters.

p.em: Example: The aestheticization of celebrity tragedies turns personal hardship into trendy background content.

cosy-blockquote.p: Viral trend ≠ Timeless tradition – a rapidly spreading online behavior that disappears quickly ≠ an enduring cultural practice passed across generations.

p.em: Example: A viral trend on photo platforms lasts only weeks, whereas a timeless tradition connects generations over centuries.

cosy-blockquote.p: Cultural icon ≠ Fleeting celebrity – a figure who symbolizes an entire era or artistic movement ≠ a person who gains temporary fame without lasting impact.

p.em: Example: A true cultural icon shapes societal values for decades, while a fleeting celebrity fades as soon as algorithms change.

cosy-blockquote.p: Collective memory ≠ Individual perception – shared pool of memories and knowledge held by a social group ≠ a single person's subjective understanding.

p.em: Example: Archival memorial posts contribute to collective memory by standardizing how a generation remembers a star.

cosy-blockquote.p: Morbid curiosity ≠ Empathetic concern – an unhealthy fascination with death, grief, or disturbing themes ≠ genuine compassion for another's suffering.

p.em: Example: Speculating about a star's health stems from morbid curiosity rather than empathetic concern for their well-being.

cosy-blockquote.p: Commercialized grief ≠ Quiet remembrance – monetizing or exploiting loss for clicks, views, or merchandise sales ≠ peaceful, unadvertised reflection.

p.em: Example: Online platforms thrive on commercialized grief through engagement metrics, suppressing quiet remembrance.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Does expressing parasocial grief ≠ private mourning on social media help people process personal sadness or is it an illusion of intimacy? Rarely do we examine why online tributes spread so quickly.
★ Have you ever felt genuinely saddened by the passing or retirement of a public figure you never met?

How can users distinguish between a performative tribute ≠ sincere homage when scrolling through aesthetic memorial posts?
★ Do you usually share posts when a famous artist passes away, or do you prefer quiet reflection?

Why does short-form video media generate such a powerful wave of digital nostalgia ≠ historical memory for eras people never lived through?
★ Is there a decade in music or fashion that you feel nostalgic for despite being born much later?

Is it fair that cultural creators often receive posthumous reverence ≠ lifetime appreciation while struggling for recognition during their lives?
★ Can you think of an artist whose work you only began appreciating after they passed away or retired?

What happens to human empathy when social media algorithms promote the aestheticization ≠ authentic portrayal of real tragedies?
★ Do you feel black-and-white filters and melancholic music make news stories feel less real?

Why does a viral trend ≠ timeless tradition around celebrity memorial photos catch fire so quickly on visual platforms?
★ How quickly do you get tired of seeing the exact same meme format or photo trend on your feed?

What separates a true cultural icon ≠ fleeting celebrity when we evaluate who deserves long-term public remembrance?
★ Which living musician or actor do you think will still be remembered 100 years from now?

How do digital platforms shape collective memory ≠ individual perception when everyone sees the same curated tribute edits?
★ Have online photos or documentary clips ever changed your opinion about a famous historical figure?

Where is the boundary line between innocent curiosity and morbid curiosity ≠ empathetic concern when public figures face personal crises?
★ Do you avoid clicking on gossip news stories about celebrity health issues or personal downfalls?

Is the rise of commercialized grief ≠ quiet remembrance an inevitable result of platforms monetizing user engagement metrics?
★ Should social media companies turn off advertising revenue on tribute hashtags and memorial pages?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Modern social media platforms transform parasocial grief ≠ private mourning into a public broadcast, whereas traditional societies treated grief as a solemn personal duty.
★ Do you think sharing sorrow online brings people closer or makes mourning feel superficial?

Online tribute culture encourages a performative tribute ≠ sincere homage mindset where users care more about feed aesthetics than the artist's actual legacy.
★ Have you ever posted something on social media mostly because it fit your profile's aesthetic look?

Algorithm-driven digital nostalgia ≠ historical memory creates a romanticized fantasy of the past that distorts young people's view of history.
★ Do you believe life was simpler and more romantic before smartphones existed?

Society's tendency toward posthumous reverence ≠ lifetime appreciation proves that we only value creators once they can no longer produce new work.
★ Is there a local or independent artist you actively support today to ensure they are appreciated now?

The constant aestheticization ≠ authentic portrayal of human tragedy on video platforms desensitizes viewers to genuine real-world suffering.
★ Do fast-paced news edits make tragic events feel more like a movie than reality?

A fast-moving viral trend ≠ timeless tradition replaces meaningful cultural rites with temporary internet trends that fade in days.
★ What traditional cultural ritual do you hope will survive into the next century?

Modern media elevates a cultural icon ≠ fleeting celebrity based on algorithmic reach rather than enduring artistic contribution.
★ Do modern pop stars have the same cultural power that legends like David Bowie or Whitney Houston had?

Corporate platforms shape collective memory ≠ individual perception by deciding which archival photo posts get pushed into recommended feeds.
★ Do you trust social media algorithms to show you an unbiased picture of world events?

Exploiting celebrity health scares out of morbid curiosity ≠ empathetic concern reveals a toxic side of modern spectator culture.
★ Should paparazzi and gossip blogs face strict legal limits when photographing public figures in crisis?

Turning public loss into commercialized grief ≠ quiet remembrance damages our collective moral compass in favor of tech company profits.
★ How can individuals protect their mental space from constant sensationalized digital content?

ul.li: Incorrect: Rarely people think → Correct: Rarely do people think ((Grammar inversion: Negative adverb 'rarely' requires auxiliary verb inversion 'do people think'))
Incorrect: Many fans → Correct: Many fans ((Word order: Transitive verb + direct object + temporal adverbial modifier))
Incorrect: We talked about → Correct: We discussed X ((Lexical choice & deletion: 'discuss' is transitive and does not take preposition 'about'))
